variant.text: Task data originates from MIMIC-IV v2.2, a PhysioNet snapshot from January 2023. Each task record preserves the source patient identifier, enabling complete traceability from any task back to its underlying patient record.

The source database consists of de-identified patient records collected between 2008 and 2019 from routine hospital care. Distribution follows a credentialed data use agreement, and the originating institution's IRB approved a consent waiver for this research.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.

The benchmark includes a safety test suite that measures unsafe outputs such as contraindicated medication orders, and a separate bias test that compares agent accuracy across patient demographic groups.

To limit contamination, the test split is held out and distributed only through gated access, and we measured verbatim overlap between the test tasks and a public web corpus, finding no exact matches.
Ground-truth answers are used by the evaluator to compute scores after each episode.

Environment components are fixed at release: database snapshot, software image, and patient-simulation LLM are each version-pinned. During evaluation, only the model under test is called; no other external services are involved.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
Grading validates both intended state modifications and preservation of unrelated records. Any unintended changes are caught and scored as failures.
Random-action agents achieve 3.1% success across tasks. Appendix tables document baseline success rates for each metric.
All runs use temperature 0 and a fixed random seed, and each task is run three times; this repeated-run policy is described in the main text.
We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all model scores and test the difference between the two best models with a paired permutation test (p = 0.02).
Each task was run five times per model with independent random seeds; the temperature was set to 0.7, and the reported scores are means over the five independent runs.
Headline scores carry 95% bootstrap CIs where the resampling unit is the task. When multiple tasks share a patient, the bootstrap resamples patients to address within-patient clustering.

To measure reliability, we ran each task eight times and report pass^8, the fraction of tasks solved in all eight runs, together with the agreement of the final environment state across the eight runs.

Models were queried through their APIs using the snapshot identifiers gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, with temperature 0 and a maximum of 2,048 output tokens; all reported numbers correspond to harness release v1.2.0.

Tools are specified using JSON schemas with name, arguments, and types. Documentation for each tool declares whether it reads or modifies state and describes return values, including error messages for invalid arguments. Agent prompts include these tool descriptions.

Conformance testing confirms tool behavior matches documentation. Two tools consist of simulated stubs providing fixed placeholder responses. This is disclosed both in the paper and in the tool descriptions visible to the agent.
The grader takes the final environment state as its input. We validated the grader on 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, finding a false-accept rate of 1% and a false-reject rate of 2%.

Agents have no web access during runs and retrieval tools are restricted to the task environment, so answers cannot leak through external search. A private held-out split with hidden labels is kept off all public surfaces, and every released task carries a canary string.
We report accuracy per task family (diagnosis, ordering and documentation tasks) and per patient subgroup by sex and race, and each table lists the number of cases in every slice.

The patient records are real de-identified records from a hospital database. Their use was approved under a data use agreement requiring credentialed access and de-identification by the safe harbour method, and the data are released under terms separate from the MIT code licence.
